assessment: The incumbent supplies assembled, rearrangeable organizers with no recorded damage claims (D2-O7), but observed time, component reports and unaided arrangement fall short of the intended outcomes (D2-O2–O4). Assembly, selection, checking and instruction problems remain plausible contributors; their shares are unmeasured. Repeated three-compartment orders taking seven to nine minutes while mixed batches contain every extreme delay supports investigating order variation, but does not separate switching from layout complexity (D2-O6). A concrete limiting observation is overlapping widths among first-attempt and retry partitions (D2-O5): width alone cannot cleanly classify insertion difficulty. No mechanism is established.

openings.claim: Order switching and shared-bin selection may contribute to delays and component errors; temporary order-specific staging with a component-count check may reduce both.
openings.delta: Test selection and checking separately from insertion, while retaining full assembly and every accepted configuration.
openings.prediction: For comparable layouts and workers, staged orders have shorter selection/checking times and fewer independently detected component discrepancies; unchanged insertion time would distinguish this account from an insertion bottleneck.
openings.probe: Use up to 15 sample organizers in matched, counterbalanced current-versus-staged cycles across layouts and both workers. Record each work stage, staging overhead, color and component correctness. Reuse samples; inspect for wear. Cost staging before adoption and measure total assembly/packing time, including staging.
assumptions: Temporary staging fits the existing bench and stated budgets.
Testing and any rollout fit the fixed delivery date.
Repeated sample handling does not materially distort timings.

openings.claim: Does a diagram showing the ordered layout resolve short-partition confusion when contents are independently verified complete?
openings.delta: Discriminate instruction ambiguity from difficulties persisting with correct parts and layout-specific guidance.
openings.prediction: Instruction ambiguity predicts fewer placement questions with the ordered-layout diagram; persistent confusion would weaken that account.
openings.probe: Randomly assign ten participants, balanced by layout, to current or ordered-layout diagrams using verified-complete samples. Record unaided success, time and exact failure step. Treat five per condition as exploratory, then verify pilot outcomes separately.
assumptions: Diagram substitution fits cost and delivery limits.
Samples preserve footprint, assortment, removable partitions, selected counts and color.
